However, fully remote studies lack face-to-face interaction, which may affect motivation, particularly in the delivery of personalized nutritional advice. Additionally, self-reported data may vary in terms of standardization and completeness. Objective: The study’s primary objective is to evaluate the feasibility of conducting a fully remote, fully digital randomized controlled nutritional intervention, including participant experience and the capability to perform do-it-yourself anthropometric measurements at home. Secondary objectives are to determine whether self-collected data could detect changes in body weight and other anthropometric outcomes, and to compare the effectiveness of generic versus personalized nutrition advice, with and without personalized food boxes. Methods: We conducted a fully online, 3-arm randomized controlled trial including adults with overweight or obesity who were motivated to lose weight. Participants were assigned to a control group that received generic advice (n=43), a personalized intervention group that received personalized advice only (n=40), or a personalized intervention plus group that received personalized advice plus personalized food boxes (n=39). The 6-week intervention was delivered entirely digitally, and all anthropometric measurements, questionnaires, and dietary data were self-collected at home. Feasibility was assessed using adherence metrics, completion of self-measurements, and a user-experience questionnaire. Secondary analyses evaluated weight loss, changes in anthropometry, and exploratory associations, including sex differences. Results: Feasibility was high—102 out of 122 (83.6%) participants found the self-measured anthropometric assessments easy to perform, and 112 (91.8%) participants reported that completing questionnaires from home was easy. For secondary outcomes, participants receiving personalized, but not generic, nutritional advice significantly lost body weight (–1.0 kg; P=.002). Participants receiving personalized food boxes in addition to personalized nutritional advice lost significantly more body weight than the other 2 groups (–2.5 kg; P=.001) and also showed a decrease in hip circumference (–2.9 cm; P=.01). Personalized advice was not easier or more enjoyable to implement than generic nutritional advice, whereas the addition of personalized food boxes improved the ease of implementing personalized nutritional advice (P<.001). All participants, irrespective of the intervention arm, reduced intake of unhealthy food groups, including ready-made meals (113.6 g vs 78.5 g, –30.9%); sauces and gravy (18.8 g vs 10.0 g, –46.8%); sweet snacks (84.8 g vs 64.1 g, –24.4%); savory snacks (50.5 g vs 40.0 g, –20.1%); bread, pasta, rice, and wraps (nutritional quality score of 1.9 vs 1.7, –10.5%); and vegetables (129.0 g vs 118.7 g, –8.0%); and replaced coffee with tea. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that fully remote, participant-led nutritional intervention studies are feasible, with participants able to independently perform anthropometric measurements and self-report data of sufficient quality to detect meaningful effects. JSON: Name: remote_personalized_nutrition_rct Title: Randomized controlled evaluation of a fully remote digital personalized nutrition intervention with and without personalized meal provision for weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity Short Hypothesis: In adults with overweight or obesity, a fully remote digital personalized nutritional advice program will produce greater mean body-weight loss over 6 weeks than generic nutritional advice, and adding personalized meal provision will further increase mean weight loss relative to personalized advice alone. Related Work: Prior work shows that decentralized, digital delivery can increase reach and reduce participant burden relative to clinic-based trials, and that personalized nutrition interventions often outperform generic dietary advice in short-term behavior change and weight loss. mHealth and web-based weight-loss programs reduce energy and fat intake and can improve diet quality, and some studies suggest added benefit when human coaching is included. Limitations across existing approaches include small samples, short follow-up, inconsistent validation of participant self-measurements, reliance on self-reported dietary intake, limited experimental comparison of personalized advice with and without food provision, and unclear generalizability to fully remote, participant-led trial designs. The combined effects of personalization and direct meal provision in a fully remote randomized design, including validation of self-collected anthropometrics and sex-stratified responses, remain unresolved. Abstract: Problem: Fully remote digital nutritional trials promise scale and low participant burden but raise questions about data quality, participant adherence, and whether personalized advice delivered online retains efficacy versus generic guidance. Approach: Conduct a 3-arm, fully remote randomized controlled trial (control: generic advice; P: personalized digital advice; PP: personalized advice plus personalized meal boxes) with participant-collected anthropometrics and web-based dietary assessment at weeks 0, 2, 4, and 6. Main contribution: Provide a validated protocol and empirical evidence on (1) feasibility and internal validity of DIY anthropometric measures and remote questionnaires, (2) comparative effectiveness of personalized versus generic digital advice, and (3) incremental effect of personalized meal provision. Expected outcome: Demonstrate whether self-collected data are sufficiently reliable to detect clinically relevant short-term weight change, quantify effect sizes for personalized interventions with and without meal provision, and identify sex-specific response patterns to inform scalable remote nutrition trials. Experiments: Design: Parallel-group randomized controlled trial with three arms: Control (generic dietary advice), Personalized (digital, tailored caloric and macronutrient targets + digital meal tracking), Personalized+Provision (same personalization plus personalized meal boxes for 5/7 days). Sample: Recruit 180 adults aged 25-60 with BMI 25-40 kg/m2 motivated to lose weight, stratified randomization by sex, age band, and BMI category. Target analyzable N ~150 (accounting for 15-20% dropout). Measurements: Self-measured weight, waist, hip at weeks 0,2,4,6 via app with instructional video; Nutri+ food-frequency module at baseline and week 6; PAL via validated questionnaire at each visit; adherence logs and app engagement metrics continuously. Validation sub-study: n=30 subset performs in-person anthropometrics at weeks 0 and 6 to quantify measurement bias and variance. Baselines: generic advice arm. Baseline covariates: age, sex, baseline weight, PAL, habitual dietary intake. Primary outcome: mean change in body weight (kg) from baseline to week 6. Secondary outcomes: change in BMI, waist and hip circumferences, waist-to-hip ratio, proportion achieving >=3% and >=5% weight loss, changes in targeted food group intake, adherence rates, user-experience scores. Metrics and tests: mixed-effects linear model for repeated measures with fixed effects (group, time, group*time) and random intercepts; intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses; ANCOVA for week-6 outcomes adjusted for baseline; Pearson correlations for self-measured vs in-person validation; subgroup analyses by sex; multiple-testing correction for secondary endpoints. Ablation/Comparisons: (1) P vs Control to test personalization effect; (2) PP vs P to isolate meal provision impact; (3) validation sub-study comparing DIY versus in-person measures; (4) sensitivity analyses excluding participants with low adherence. Sample size/power: powered (80%) to detect 1.0 kg between-group difference (SD=1.8 kg) at alpha=0.05 requiring ~44 participants per arm; plan for 60 per arm to account for attrition. Risk Factors and Limitations: Selection bias toward digitally literate and motivated participants limits generalizability. Self-reported anthropometrics and dietary intake may contain systematic measurement error and social desirability bias; validation sub-study may not fully capture population-level misreporting. Differential attrition across arms (e.g., higher burden in non-provision arms) can bias per-protocol estimates and reduce power. Providing personalized meal boxes introduces an incentive/confounder (free meals) that may increase engagement independent of nutritional personalization. Short duration (6 weeks) limits inference about long-term weight maintenance. Scalability and cost constraints exist for meal provision interventions. Randomization imbalance due to dropout or exclusion may occur despite stratification. External factors (seasonality, local food availability) and unmeasured behavioral covariates (stress, concurrent dieting) can confound outcomes. Regulatory, logistical, and data privacy constraints in remote data collection may restrict recruitment and data linkage.
